# Schedule social posts: Slack & Airtable for scheduling

**Pattern:** Social Scheduler · **Level:** Expert · **Trigger:** Scheduled

## Overview

Runs on a schedule, and covers scheduling work end to end across Slack and Airtable.

It moves through 17 working steps plus a 2-node error rail, in this order:

1. Hourly Schedule
2. Read Content Calendar (Airtable)
3. Due for Publishing?
4. Post One at a Time
5. Publish to Slack
6. Space Out Posts
7. Mark Row Published
8. Count Published
9. Stamp Processing Time
10. Tag Pipeline Metadata
11. Sort Posts Newest First
12. Save Execution Metadata
13. Guard Non-Empty content
14. Cap Batch Volume
15. Summarize Run Stats
16. Append Audit Row (Airtable)
17. Send Summary to Slack

Anything that throws leaves the happy path at that node and goes down the red rail — Capture Failure Context → Escalate Failure to Slack — so a failure is reported rather than silently lost.

## Why it exists

Doing scheduling work by hand is slow and easy to get wrong, and it stops entirely when the person who does it is away. This makes the process repeatable and monitored, with failures surfaced instead of silently lost.

## Main flow

Hourly Schedule → Read Content Calendar (Airtable) → Due for Publishing? → Post One at a Time → Publish to Slack → Space Out Posts → Mark Row Published → Count Published → Stamp Processing Time → Tag Pipeline Metadata → Sort Posts Newest First → Save Execution Metadata → Guard Non-Empty content → Cap Batch Volume → Summarize Run Stats → Append Audit Row (Airtable) → Send Summary to Slack → Capture Failure Context → Escalate Failure to Slack

## Use it for

- Teams keeping Slack and Airtable aligned by hand for scheduling
- Scheduling sequences that run over days and must survive a restart before Slack
- A backlog too large to push into Slack in one pass, across 19 nodes
- Scheduling work where "Read Content Calendar (Airtable)" is still a manual step before Slack

## You get

- Keeps Slack and Airtable in step for scheduling, without anyone re-typing a row
- A failed Slack or Airtable call is retried rather than dropped, at any of the 19 nodes in this scheduling build
- The pause before Slack is durable — a scheduling run survives a restart
- Batches the work so Slack rate limits never break a scheduling run
- Every scheduling run leaves an audit row behind, alongside Slack

## Before first run
Connect credentials: Airtable PAT; Slack OAuth2.
Follow the color key: 🟦 entry · 🟪 AI · 🟫 actions · ⬜ utilities · 🟩 outputs · 🟥 error rail.
Each node has its own doc card underneath — read those before editing.

## Try it now
Sample data is pinned on the trigger — hit **Execute Workflow** to watch it flow through every node before connecting any real credentials. Unpin the trigger (right-click → Unpin) when you're ready to go live.

## Design decisions

Posts go out one at a time through a batch-of-1 loop with a Wait between each, not all at once — most social APIs rate-limit bursts, and spacing also just reads as more natural than five posts landing in the same second. A row is marked published only after the post succeeds, so a mid-run crash resumes cleanly instead of re-posting everything.

## Practice exercises

You've got the basics covered — push further:

1. Change the spacing delay and see how total run time scales with calendar size.
2. Add a second platform and post to both for each due item.
3. Manually mark one row as already-published and confirm the filter skips it.

## Credentials setup

Credentials are never included in a template file, so every node below needs its own connection before the first real run. In n8n: open the node, click the Credential dropdown, choose **Create new**.

**Airtable PAT**
airtable.com/create/tokens → create a Personal Access Token.
_Gotcha:_ Scope the token to the specific base, and grant `data.records:write`. Field names are case-sensitive.

**Slack OAuth2**
Slack API → Your Apps → create an app → OAuth & Permissions. n8n's Slack OAuth2 credential walks the install for you.
_Gotcha:_ Needs `chat:write`. Invite the bot to the channel or posting fails with `not_in_channel`.

Set each credential up once and it is reusable across every workflow in your instance.

## Troubleshooting

**Workflow does nothing when the trigger should fire**
Cause: It is still a draft, or the trigger is inactive.
Fix: Publish/activate the workflow. Manual test runs use a different URL than production.

**A node shows a red error triangle on import**
Cause: No credential is attached yet.
Fix: Expected on a fresh import — open the node and attach a credential (see the Credentials setup note).

**The loop runs forever or exits immediately**
Cause: The loop output and the done output are wired the wrong way round.
Fix: Output 2 is the loop body; output 1 fires after the last batch.

Still stuck? n8n's **Executions** tab shows the exact node that failed and the data going into it — start there rather than guessing.

## 🛟 Error handling & retries

External calls retry **3× with 2s backoff**. Anything still failing exits through its node's error output into the red error rail → context is captured and the on-call channel is alerted. Set an n8n **Error Workflow** in settings as the final safety net.

## ⏱ Rate limiting

Work is batched and spaced with Wait so provider quotas aren't tripped. If you hit 429s, lower the batch size or raise the wait — throughput drops, reliability rises.

## 🛠 Customize me

Quick wins: point the data nodes at your own accounts (see 🔑 lines on each card), adjust the trigger cadence, and tune thresholds/labels to your scheduling process. Every node card explains its role — safe to extend at any marked branch.

## 🔐 Security

Credentials live in n8n's credential store and are never written into node parameters — that is why this file carries none.

**Least privilege for this build**
- Slack: `chat:write` is enough to post. Do not add `channels:history` unless a node here actually reads messages.
- Airtable: scope the PAT to this one base and to `data.records:write`; a token scoped to the workspace can rewrite every base.

**Do not log**
Log the identifier and the outcome, not the whole scheduling payload. n8n stores execution data verbatim, so anything a node emits is readable by everyone with instance access.
